units.translation: The examples of the verb εἰμί [I am] collected by Wellauer, since most of them are of such a kind that it is not worth the trouble to write out the words with which they are read in connection, we indicate by line numbers alone, arranged according to the order of tenses and moods. Two classes of these examples, however, must be distinguished. For εἰμί [I am] is either a substantive verb, which signifies to be, i.e. to exist, something, and contains the predicate in itself, or it is the copula, as logicians call it, which requires the addition of some predicate. Where it is a copula, in the present indicative of all persons, with the single exception of the second person εἶ [you are], the accent is thrown back (according to the doctrine of the grammarians, which Hermann in his work on the emendation of Greek grammar p. 84 ff. and Buttmann in his Greek Grammar vol. 1 p. 552 have expounded) when the preceding word is of such a kind that the accent can be thrown back upon it, as ἕτοιμός εἰμι [I am ready], ἕτοιμός ἐστι [he is ready], but it is retained where it cannot be thrown back, as σώφρων εἰμί [I am prudent], σώφρων ἐστί [he is prudent]. Moreover, the grammarians (cited by Fischer in his notes on Weller's Grammar vol. 1 p. 294) prescribe that the third person ἐστί [he/she/it is] should be written with the accent drawn back, ἔστιν [he/she/it is], at the beginning of a sentence, in a question, after the words ἀλλ' [but] and τοῦτ' [this] (where the second syllable has been elided), εἰ [if], καί [and], μή [not], οὐκ [not], ὡς [as], μέν [indeed], ὅτι [that], and in the formulas ἔστιν ὅς [there is someone who], ἔστιν ὅτε [there is a time when], ἔστιν ὅπου [there is a place where], ἔστιν ὅπως [there is a way in which], ἔστιν ὡς [there is a sense in which] and the like: which rules are observed with sufficient accuracy in the manuscripts and are undoubtedly true regarding the formulas just mentioned and the particles without accent εἰ [if], οὐκ [not], ὡς [as], but are hardly probable and lack a suitable reason regarding the others ἀλλ' [but], τοῦτ' [this], καί [and], μή [not], μέν [indeed], ὅτι [that], as Buttmann also in part has noticed.
